wa_mount_cruiser_south_corner.rappels: Most parties make three rappels on a single 60 m rope used doubled: about 25 m from the newer bolted anchor on the ridge crest down to the platform, then two of about 30 m down the Class 4 gully past the chockstone to its base. Some parties rappel twice and downclimb the lower gully instead. A second rope makes linking the stations easier but is not required.

rappel_detail.pull: Short — the least demanding of the tower rappels, and the one that sets expectations too low for the three above it.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off a major gendarme on the ridge crest, on the way up the buttress.
rappel_detail.station: Off the first tower on the ridge.

rappel_detail.pull: About 40 m, so a single 60 m doubled does not reach. Parties either carry a second line, or rappel as far as one rope allows and then build a second station or belay the last stretch of low fifth class down to the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Continues past another pinnacle; anchors are improvised rather than fixed stations.
rappel_detail.station: Off the second tower into the notch below it.

rappel_detail.pull: About 40 m again — same problem and same two workarounds if you are on a single rope.
rappel_detail.notes: Rockfall risk noted along this ridge; back up marginal-looking anchors where possible.

rappel_detail.pull: Closer to 50 m, the longest of the tower rappels. On one rope this is the one most likely to leave you hanging above the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Getting off this notch/gendarme is effectively irreversible once ropes are pulled.

Rappel 5 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.

rappel_detail.pull: Carry a good length of cord. The single-strand anchors left here have been found in poor shape a year later, and have since been rebuilt redundant — assume you will be replacing rather than clipping.
rappel_detail.notes: Off the Pole of Remoteness, the last major tower before the false summit; easier ground then leads toward West Fury's summit.
hazards: Rockfall on this rappel severed a rope on the first ascent. Having a second line in the system is what made that survivable
rappel_detail.station: Off the top of the Pole of Remoteness. The anchor is a large block on the summit of the tower; parties have tested it deliberately before committing to it.

wa_mount_fury_east_mongo_ridge.rappels: At least a dozen rappels documented on the first ascent, mostly double-rope raps off the lower towers and gendarmes. No fixed anchors — natural gear and tat only.
wa_mount_fury_east_mongo_ridge.rappel_count_note: Roughly a dozen rappels (12-13) are described getting off gendarmes/pinnacles along Mongo Ridge; a rap rope has been reported severed by rockfall on a marginal anchor somewhere along this stretch, so treat every anchor with suspicion. Individual rappel lengths are not known, so no per-station length is shown.

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.rappels: 2-5 rappels through the Kautz ice chute, depending on conditions and how much rope you carry: 1-3 down the upper ice step and 1-2 down the lower one, all on V-thread anchors you thread yourself. The four stations listed here are a representative middle count for a party on a single 60 m rope - fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.rappel_count_note: The count ranges from 2-5 rappels total, depending on rope length/number of ropes carried: 1-3 on the upper ice step, 1-2 on the lower ice step. 4 is used here as a representative middle count for a party on a single 60m rope; fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.descent_text: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length and how many ropes the team carries, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, fewer with two ropes or more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.rappels: 2-5 rappels through the Kautz ice steps on the way down, depending on conditions and how much rope you carry: 1-3 down the upper ice step and 1-2 down the lower one, all on ice anchors you build yourself. The four stations listed are a middle count for a party on a single 60 m rope; with two 60 m ropes it can be as few as two, plus some downclimbing.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.rappel_count_note: The count ranges from 2-5 rappels total, depending on rope length/number of ropes carried: 1-3 on the upper ice step, 1-2 on the lower ice step. 4 is used here as a representative middle count for a party on a single 60m rope; fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching. With two 60 m ropes, two double-rope rappels plus some downclimbing get most parties through the steepest ice.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.descent_text: Descent is normally either back down the Kautz Glacier itself (the way you came) or a carryover down the Disappointment Cleaver route to Paradise. On the headwall's ice steps specifically, with 60m ropes two double-rope rappels plus some downclimbing are enough to get back down through the steepest sections to the base of the ice pitches — rappel anchors on the ice steps are typically ice (V-thread/zero-thread) anchors, the modern standard, not fixed bolts — old ascent-placed threads should not be reused. Expect 1-3 rappels through the upper step and 1-2 more through the lower step. This is a snow/ice route with no permanent hardware. In marginal conditions, some parties place running belays or fix a line through the ice steps instead of full rappels, both for the descent and to assist less-experienced members. Below the headwall, the Kautz/Wilson Glacier descent back to the Turtle or out via Comet Falls involves standard roped glacier travel, not further rappelling.
